Photograph: WPA/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Yvette Cooper summarised Keir Starmer’s leadership as ‘bring me solutions, not problems’. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images Yvette Cooper Yvette Cooper says Labour ‘did not do government very well’ under Starmer Health secretary praises more collegiate style under Andy Burnham and says previous No 10 sidelined her from key policy launch Rowena Mason Whitehall editor Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Yvette Cooper admits Labour has “not done government very well” in the last couple of years, and accused Keir Starmer’s No 10 of sidelining her during the launch of a key immigration policy when she was home secretary. Speaking on the Political Currency podcast with the former Conservative chancellor George Osborne, Cooper highlighted some of the difficulties ministers faced with Starmer’s leadership, which she summarised as “bring me solutions, not problems”. She said she had found a more collegiate style under Andy Burnham , and argued in favour of trying to form a national consensus around social care and reintroducing Sure Start-style children’s centres for young families under his leadership. Contrasting the new prime minister with Starmer, the health secretary said there had been “a style of leading the government that maybe doesn’t necessarily work in politics” under the last administration. As an example, she was critical of how she was in effect excluded from launching the immigration white paper in May 2025 while home secretary. At the launch, which was fronted by Starmer, he spoke of introducing policies to deal with the risk that Britain could become an “island of strangers”, which Cooper later had to defend. She told Osborne: “Keir wanted the immigration white paper. Actually, we did a lot of the work on it in the Home Office, and a whole set of plans to bring legal migration back under control, a whole set of reforms around illegal migration and so on. “But then No 10 wanted Keir to announce it on his own and to front that up, and so I didn’t see what was going to be said or what the announcement was … that was the way that No 10 operated. “It was like, well, you can sit in the front row of the launch, but actually the prime minister is going to launch it.” She added: “I think Keir’s style of leadership was ‘bring me solutions, not problems’. And I’m not sure you can do that in politics … the thing you see with Andy is ‘hang on, bring me the problems. I want to talk to you about the problems. I want to engage. I want to hear about the problems, and I want us to work together in solving them.’” Cooper contrasted Starmer’s desire to be presented with a set of options with Burnham’s more discursive approach on social care, saying he was “passionate about it” and wanted to talk about the problems and how to solve them. “He wanted me to be part of the event, launching it, to be speaking at it, to be talking about it,” she said. “I think Keir’s style of leadership, which is very effective in other ways, actually, was … it just didn’t fit with that emotion that you need to drive change and involve people and include people in politics.” During the podcast, Cooper also spoke about her ambition to build a consensus around a solution to the social care crisis, saying it was about “trying to create a sense that somebody’s going to have to solve this, and you know if it’s not this government, it’s going to have to be the next government, or we’re going to end up with a never-ending, growing crisis for our NHS because we’re not doing things to solve social care”. She said she also wanted to build national agreement around the principles of Sure Start, a programme to help young families that was cut when Osborne was chancellor. Telling Osborne she was “still angry” about his decision to cut funding for Sure Start children’s centres, she said: “I actually want to build that same national consensus on how we start our kids’ lives, so that no future government of whatever party would think, you know what, it’s OK to rip up Sure Start, because actually we establish this as something that’s so important in children’s lives.” Explore more on these topics Yvette Cooper Labour Keir Starmer Andy Burnham news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr4g.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, More than 500 schools were partially or totally closed by protests on Monday, the French education minister said By Tinshui Yeung Published 6 hours ago France is braced for major protests on Tuesday, after organisers called for a nationwide day of action in support of students demanding more investment in education. It comes after a week of demonstrations, which saw students blockading hundreds of schools, at least 190 students injured, and more than 5,000 people arrested. One student had his hand blown off during a confrontation on Monday, while another was reportedly struck in the head by a tear gas grenade last week. France's prime minister said the government had announced measures to address their demands, but the Union Syndicale LycÃ©enne (USL), a major organiser of the protests, said the government had offered "nothing concrete". The organisation called on people to join their mobilisation on Tuesday in the face of "this political deadlock and what we describe as unprecedented repression of the movement". Some other organisations have also shown their support for the students, with the teachers' union SNES-FSU urging its members to join Tuesday's protest. The radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a year of major unrest, which saw millions of workers go on strike. The wave of demonstrations began in September in Paris and has spread across the country, with students protesting over a range of issues, including overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and a lack of teachers. The protests were started by high school students, who were later joined by university students. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Some protesters launched fireworks during clashes with police in the streets near Paris on Monday On Sunday, French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu announced a series of measures to "address the difficulties faced by secondary school students and education staff", promising "visible changes" in schools. However, he also said: "We will make no concessions to violence. We stand by students and staff who have been assaulted, as well as police officers and gendarmes who have been injured." The unrest has not only seen schools blockaded, but also rubbish bins set on fire. Education Minister Ãdouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "burned and ransacked" since the start of the protests. Violent clashes between students and the police have led to some serious injuries throughout the course of the protests so far. On Monday, a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation near a school in the northern city of Lens. The student was transferred to a nearby hospital and his injury is not life-threatening, according to officials. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Protesters have set road materials on fire as barricades Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'AumÃ´ne after reportedly being struck on the head by a tear gas grenade. The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer. Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered". "It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying. "This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study." Among the 5,060 people arrested since the start of the movement, 87% were minors and 13% were adults, according to France's justice ministry , external . Fourteen people have reportedly been placed in pre-trial detention, while 1,802 people are facing prosecution, including 319 adults and 1,483 minors. The USL has accused police of using excessive force against the protesters. Responding to this allegation last week, Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said the demonstrations had been policed in "an extremely proportionate manner". Image source, Reuters Image caption, Masked protesters took to the streets near LycÃ©e Berthelot in Aubervilliers While France's next presidential election is still months away, the protests and the response by French authorities have been heavily politicised. The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for fuelling the protests. Lecornu said LFI was being "irresponsible" in calling for the movement to expand. The leader of the hard-right National Rally, Marine Le Pen, has also criticised the left for its response. "This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organised by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise," she said, calling for a new anti-rioting law to be passed. Meanwhile MÃ©lenchon, the LFI's party's presidential candidate, has been blaming the police for "abuses of power", calling on people to take to the streets to "protect the youth demonstrations". The left-wing mayor of Marseille, BenoÃ®t Payan, condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves calmly, he said. https://telex.hu/sport/2026/11/08/fradi-.text: Verekedés tört ki, ami rendőri beavatkozáshoz vezetett a vasárnapi Vasas–Ferencváros-futballmérkőzés előtt az Illovszky Rudolf Stadionnál. A Nemzeti Sport szerint a meccs előtti percekben verekedtek össze a szurkolók, a rendőrök pedig könnygázzal igyekeztek véget vetni a jelenetnek. A gáz a nézőtérre is beszivárgott, a lap szerint az ottani szurkolók is megérezték. A vasas stadionjának hazai szurkolói bejáratához mentek a vendégként szereplő FTC szurkolói, ott lett verekedés. A nézőtérre bejutó könnygáz miatt több szurkoló ott is könnyezni és köhögni kezdett. Az összetűzés nem tartott sokáig, a rendőrség beavatkozása hamar véget vetett a jelenetnek. A közösségi médiában videók is megjelentek az eseményekről.
